opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really productive methodology, with some important caveats. The appeal is obvious: if you take something like a small transformer trained on, say, modular arithmetic or a toy board game like Othello, you can actually open it up and understand, almost completely, what it's doing. You can find the circuit, characterize the representation, and test it causally. That's just not possible yet with a frontier-scale model trained on the whole internet.

And there's been surprisingly good evidence that some of what you find in the small setting carries over. The Othello work is a nice example. You see a model learn something like a world-state representation, a board, purely from predicting next moves. Then people go looking for analogous structure in big language models, things like linear representations of spatial or temporal information, or of truth values, and they find something that rhymes with it. So the toy models end up generating hypotheses you might never have thought to test otherwise.

But I'd be careful about treating them as predictive in a strong sense. The synthetic task decides what the right representation even is. In Othello there's a ground-truth board state, and the model is under a lot of pressure to recover it. Natural language doesn't give you a single clean latent variable like that. There are many overlapping, partially specified world states, and large models seem to represent them in messier, more distributed, more superposed ways. Scale also changes things qualitatively. Some behaviors only show up at certain sizes or with certain data mixtures, and the mechanism a small model uses for a task may simply not be the one a large model uses, even when they behave the same.

So I think of small models as a source of hypotheses and a way to sharpen our tools. They tell us what kinds of representations are learnable from what kinds of signals, and they give us interpretability techniques we can validate where we know the answer. The real test is always going back to the large model and checking causally, through interventions and not just probing, whether the structure is there and whether the model actually uses it. When it holds up, that's exciting. When it doesn't, the difference is usually telling you something interesting about what scale and real data are buying you.

r001.rationale: The response describes findings from small models as evidence that some representations carry over to larger models, where they can guide hypotheses. That communicates an inductive extrapolation, while noting its limits.

r002.rationale: It says there is evidence that some findings carry over and gives analogous examples, but does not claim that representational mechanisms often recur. It also cautions that large models may use different mechanisms.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the more promising methodological bets in interpretability right now, but it comes with a specific set of caveats that I want to be careful about.

The appeal is obvious. Big models are expensive to probe, hard to intervene on, and the training distribution is so heterogeneous that it's very difficult to say what any given representation is "for." With a small model on a synthetic task, you control everything. You know the generative process, you know what the latent variables are, and you can ask crisp questions like: does the model recover the underlying state of the world, does it build something like a map, does it track who knows what. Some of the cleanest results we have about structured representations in neural networks come from exactly this setup, things like the board game work, or the little grammar induction experiments.

The question is what licenses the jump from "a 2-layer transformer trained on this toy domain does X" to "GPT-whatever does X." And I think the honest answer is that it depends on what X is. If X is a claim about an inductive bias of the architecture, the way attention composes, what kinds of circuits are cheap to learn under gradient descent, then I'm fairly optimistic the small-model result transfers, because those properties don't change much with scale. If X is a claim about what the model actually ends up representing about the world, I'm much more cautious. Large models are solving a vastly more complex prediction problem, and the representation that's optimal for predicting the next token on the whole internet might look nothing like the representation that's optimal for a clean synthetic task. We've seen cases where mechanisms found in small models are simply absent in large ones, or exist alongside a dozen competing strategies.

So the way I'd frame it is: synthetic small-model studies are hypothesis generators, and they're good at ruling things in as possible. They tell you a network can learn a world model, or can implement in-context learning via something that looks like gradient descent. What they don't do on their own is tell you that the large model does. For that you still need the second half of the loop, where you take the hypothesis back to the real model and check it with probes or causal interventions.

The other thing I'd flag is that the choice of synthetic task is where a lot of the real intellectual work happens, and it's easy to accidentally build a task where the result is baked in. If you design a dataset so that the only way to achieve low loss is to represent some variable, then finding that variable is not very surprising. The interesting cases are the ones where there's a shortcut available and the model nonetheless learns the structured thing, or vice versa. That's when you learn something about the learning process rather than about your dataset.

So, net: I'd call it a necessary tool but not a sufficient one. I'd be worried about a field that only did large-model interpretability, because you'd never be able to validate your methods against ground truth. And I'd be equally worried about a field that only did toy models, because you'd end up with beautiful theories of systems nobody uses.

r001.rationale: It frames the move from a toy-model result to a claim about a large model as a question of what licenses that transfer, and says the answer depends on the claim. That communicates an inference from small-model findings to larger models.

r002.rationale: It does not say small-model mechanisms often recur in larger models. It says some mechanisms found in small models may be absent in large ones or coexist with competing strategies.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a promising approach, but we have to be careful about what we mean by “predict.” A small synthetic task lets you isolate a particular computational problem and study how a model solves it. You can control the training data, vary the architecture, and ask whether a representation appears consistently or only under particular conditions. That’s much harder to do with a large language model.

The harder step is establishing that the same explanation applies at scale. A large model might solve the problem using a different mechanism, or the representation you see in the small model might be spread across several interacting components. Matching behavior doesn’t necessarily imply matching representations.

So I’d treat these experiments as a way to generate hypotheses. The compelling result would be to take a mechanism discovered in a small model, predict something specific about a larger model, and then test that prediction—ideally by intervening on the representation and seeing whether behavior changes in the way you expected. That would give us much stronger evidence than finding a resemblance after the fact.

r001.rationale: It describes using a mechanism found in a small model to predict a specific property of a larger model, treating that extrapolation as a hypothesis to test.

r002.rationale: It does not say small-model mechanisms often recur in larger models; it cautions that larger models may use different mechanisms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising way to generate hypotheses, but I’d be cautious about treating it as a reliable predictor. With a small model and a synthetic task, you can control what information is available and ask fairly precise questions about what the model has to represent to solve the problem. That’s a useful scientific setup.

The harder question is which findings survive when you change the scale, the training data, and the number of things the model is being asked to do. A representation that looks very clean in a synthetic setting might be distributed across lots of components in a larger model, or the larger model might find a different solution altogether.

So I’d want a loop where you identify a mechanism in the simple setting, make a concrete prediction about the larger model, and then test it—ideally by intervening on the representation and checking whether behavior changes in the way you predicted. The small model gives you a hypothesis you can actually work with; the evidence in the larger model is what tells you how far it generalizes.

r001.rationale: The response treats findings from a small model as hypotheses whose generalization to larger models must be tested, characterizing the move as an inductive inference.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that mechanisms found in small models often recur in larger ones; it says they may be distributed differently or the larger model may use another solution.
